12254-illustrated-history-of-furniture-f:
Frederick Litchfield published this illustrated history of furniture in 1893, tracing decorative furniture and woodwork from the earliest reliable records to his own day. Numerous illustrations show chairs, tables, cabinets, and interiors across periods.

The preface promises an account of changes in design, with a careful selection of pictures, including a French chateau interior of the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. Chapters move through Egyptian, Greek, Roman, medieval, Renaissance, and modern styles, noting how craft, material, and fashion shaped each age. Litchfield writes for collectors and householders alike. The book remains a handy visual survey of how rooms have been furnished.
17194-the-relations-between-religion-and:
Frederick, Bishop of Exeter, gave these eight lectures at Oxford in 1884 on the Bampton foundation, endowed by Canon John Bampton for divinity sermons. Lecture One traces scientific belief to the uniformity of nature, testing Hume and Kant and finding both short. Lecture Two turns to religious belief, the voice within, and knowledge of one's own self.

Later lectures weigh how science and faith meet, clash, and correct each other, in plain pulpit prose with full texts and notes. The bishop writes as a churchman open to science, not as its foe. Readers keen on Victorian faith and science will find a calm, learned set of talks from the heart of the debate.
17207-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
William and Robert Chambers' April 3, 1852 journal leads with Imperfect Respectabilities, a witty essay on nice, well-dressed people with one small flaw in their past. The writer notes how hard it is to cut such folk. Their sunny faces, kind inquiries, and pleasant talk melt stiff resolve, even when a bad card affair or an awkward insolvency haunts memory.

The essay mixes humor with social morals, in the journal's plain, humane voice. More pieces in the same number follow its usual blend of life, thought, and fact for home readers. As a sample of Victorian social satire, the issue charms with its gentle sting at snobbery and good nature alike.
17348-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
William and Robert Chambers' April 10, 1852 journal leads with The Medieval Mania, an essay on society as a pendulum swinging back to old tastes. Black-letter type returns to fashion, rude nature beats refinement, and perfection is sought in the darkness of the middle ages. The writer grants Georgian art much that was tame, yet warns that reform is one thing and revolution another.

Nature, he urges, should teach through cultivated feeling, not drag readers back to forms out of place in the nineteenth century. The essay predicts a violent reaction to come. As Victorian cultural criticism, the piece is witty, firm, and still apt for any age of retro fashion.
18382-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
Number 433 of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, new series, dated Saturday, April 17, 1852, cost a penny and a half. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly, which mixed tales, essays, and useful knowledge for a wide readership. This number opens with The Dingy House, a London mystery in the magazine's plain, observant style.

London, the writer says, is like a large company where the master must introduce many people to each other, and a man may live doors from wonders he never hears of. In Great Windmill Street near the Haymarket stands a large, dingy house, detached and not in ordinary tenants' hands, near a smart, whitened haunt of gaiety. Women in wide black cloaks arrive with heavy packages, enter with caution, and are seen no more that day. Readers get a city mystery: a house, a street, and neighbors who ask no questions.
19417-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
This number of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal dates from late April of eighteen fifty-two, edited by William and Robert Chambers. Its lead piece attacks London puffery, the ads and agents that force themselves on every visitor, and leaves the reader longing for one day free of sales talk.

Other items explain artists' monograms, from simple name contractions to fancy marks, tracing a habit back to ancient makers. The journal's blend of protest, fact, and curiosity shows why Chambers' penny press won a wide British readership. A sea piece follows the brig Vincejo, eighteen guns under Captain Long, as she gives chase to a strange ship.
26170-diaries-of-sir-moses-and-lady-mont:
Edited by Dr. L. Loewe and published at Chicago in 1890, this first of two volumes draws on the diaries of Sir Moses Montefiore and his wife Judith, Lady Montefiore, covering the years 1812 to 1883. It adds Sir Moses's addresses and speeches, his letters to ministers, ambassadors, and public bodies, and his own accounts of missions undertaken in the cause of humanity.

The volume also prints firmans and edicts of eastern monarchs, his views on finance, politics, and religion, and anecdotes of the men of his time. Loewe, who had served on the 1840 mission to Damascus and Constantinople, edited the papers with his son. The book offers a long, personal record of a famous Jewish philanthropist's public life.
958-rinkitink-in-oz-wherein-is-recorded-:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Oz tale of Prince Inga of Pingaree and King Rinkitink, on a perilous quest in the magical isles beyond the borderland of Oz. Inga, a boy hero new to readers, seeks to free his parents, while Rinkitink, a fat, jolly king, aids him with humour and a magic pearl.

Baum tells the quest with warmth and wit, as the pair face the Nome King and other perils, and Inga's courage grows. The book, introduced as a story with a boy hero, stands apart from Dorothy's Oz, yet it shares its heart. Rinkitink in Oz charms readers who like quests led by a boy and a merry king.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-431-volu:
Imperfect respectabilities trap the narrator of number 431, dated April 3, 1852. A glittering-eyed bore holds him through talk of the money-market. His own troubles vanish under the flow. The handshake at parting feels like escape. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal turns that social snare into its lead sketch, wry about how kind the world is to bores.

Tales of the coast-guard and a piece called The Last Revel supply rougher company. Air-travelling looks upward, a day at the baths of Lucca looks abroad, and twenty-four hours of a sailor's life at sea looks outward. Facts about oyster-eating, the oases of Libya, and the influence of example close a number that ranges from drawing room to desert.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-432-volu:
Medieval revival in art and religion opens number 432, dated April 10, 1852. Revived monasteries are one symptom. Working men claiming old protections are another. Painters copying the middle ages are a third. The writer calls it all one mania. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal presses the charge before turning to stranger weather.

Dust-showers and red rain get a scientific airing, and a legend of Amen-Corner a literary one. The city inquest for the poor, London cab reform, and colonial penny-postage handle city business. A surveying voyage of the Rattlesnake, a celebrated French clockmaker, and Saint Elizabeth of Bohemia widen the field. Notes for intending emigrants and an emigrant's manual speak to readers planning to leave.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-433-volu:
Two women in wide black cloaks slip each day into a London mansion. They are seen no more till tomorrow. The dingy house of number 433, dated April 17, 1852, builds its tale on that mystery. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal admits that in London even neighbours ask nothing, and then sets out to satisfy the curiosity it has raised.

The late Emperor of China is profiled, and a glimpse of Ballyvourney takes readers to Ireland. The Daughter of the Bardi carries the fiction to Italy. An ayah, the Indian nurse of colonial households, is described for home readers. Small investments, the pleasures of literature, a missing ship, and wild animals in confinement complete a number strong on households, hidden and otherwise.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-434-volu:
Puff, the advertising monster, rampages through number 434, dated April 24, 1852. No lane or beech covert is safe, the lead essay complains. The shop's demon has driven out the dryads. Every beauty spot has become a billboard. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal calls puff the megatherium, the giant sloth, of modern society.

Recollections of a police-officer give the law's view of the same streets. A monomaniac and a tale called The Vincejo's Prize supply the fiction. Painters' monograms — the small marks by which artists signed work — get a collector's treatment. Things talked of in London and a sonnet finish the number. Commerce, crime, and art share one crowded Saturday, as usual in this weekly.
doe-osti-17152730-report-on-the-mesoscal:
Sourabh Kadambi, Mathew Swisher, Jia-Hong Ke, and Idaho National Laboratory colleagues model how the internal structure of 3D printed 316 stainless steel evolves under irradiation, in a September 2026 report. Radiation knocks atoms out of place, and the defects gather into clusters and cavities that swell and weaken the metal. Printed steel starts with its own fine structure, which steers that damage.

Two model families do the work. Mean field cluster dynamics follows defect populations over time, showing how dislocation density and carbon content, which slows vacancy motion, change the outcome. Spatial models then grow cavities in place, comparing sharp interface and phase field treatments and testing composition effects. Parameters were checked against data for both neutron and ion irradiation cases.
doe-osti-2498401-arm-trajectories-data-s:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report DOE/SC-ARM-TR-314, by Israel Silber, Jennifer Comstock, Michael Kieburtz, Kenneth Gaustad, and Fan Mei in August 2026, documents the ARM Trajectories data set. The product traces where air parcels came from and where they go, starting at Atmospheric Radiation Measurement deployment sites. Seven related data sets serve work on aerosols, clouds, and the planetary boundary layer.

Trajectories are computed with the HYSPLIT model, fed by the ERA5 reanalysis at its finest grid spacing of about 31 kilometers. Runs start from several points around each site, forming an ensemble for every sample. Ensemble means and spreads give both the path and an uncertainty estimate for position, temperature, and other fields. Separate data sets cover surface air, cloud layers, the boundary layer, research flights, and balloon flights.
doe-osti-2583515-national-energy-educati:
CRADA final report NREL/TP-5500-94247, dated December 18, 2024, covers NREL's partnership with the National Energy Education Development Project. Taylor Ryan was the laboratory's contact; Mary Spruill represented NEED. The work supported the Building Technologies Office's student competitions, which recruit the next generation of building scientists by letting students design and build for real.

The flagship is the Solar Decathlon, running since 2002. Collegiate teams design and construct highly efficient buildings powered by on-site renewable energy, then face judging across ten contests. The competition teaches building science careers by doing, and shows the visiting public that an efficient home can also be comfortable and desirable. NEED, the nation's long-standing energy education network, brings the teacher and student reach. The partnership described here is the connective tissue between a federal competition and the classrooms it hopes to inspire.
doe-osti-2583541-unitary-thermal-energy-:
UTEMPRA, unitary thermal energy management for propulsion range augmentation, attacked a quiet EV problem: separate heating and cooling loops wasting energy. Report NREL/TP-5400-95222, dated April 1, 2025, closes CRADA CRD-15-00578 with MAHLE Behr. Jason Lustbader was NREL's contact. Electric vehicles carry independent cooling systems for motor, battery, and cabin; each draws auxiliary load, and auxiliary load is range.

The project modeled a unified thermal system instead. A baseline thermal and cabin model came first, validated against experimental data, then a full baseline vehicle model. Against those, the team simulated the UTEMPRA concept: one integrated system using heat pump operation and waste heat recovery to serve every subsystem. The aims were lower auxiliary loads, better climate control efficiency, occupant comfort kept, and powertrain thermal needs met, with fewer cooling systems to buy and carry. Range gained from plumbing is unglamorous and real.
doe-osti-2588266-thermoelectric-heat-pum:
Kyle Gluesenkamp leads a seven-author Oak Ridge team in this CRADA final report, ORNL/TM-2025/3783, for agreement NFE-21-08859, dated March 2024. Joseph Rendall, Sylas Rehbein, and four colleagues share the work. The product is a water heater that swaps the usual vapor-compression heat pump for a thermoelectric one, aiming at mass market prices with 30 percent energy savings.

Thermoelectric modules move heat with no moving parts and no refrigerant, but they have rarely carried a whole water heater. Here a modified unit used the thermoelectric heat pump as its primary heating method. In a 24-hour test run under conditions similar to the federal rating procedure, the modules supplied all the tank heating while running about three quarters of the time. The uniform energy factor rose as a result. The report walks through the prototype build, its controls, and the measured performance.
doe-osti-2999119-leveraging-artificial-i:
Coleman Cariker and Alex Belianinov of Sandia National Laboratories report a machine learning trial in SAND2025-12414R. A eutectic alloy melts at one sharp temperature, lower than either ingredient alone, which makes such alloys handy for solders and casting. Finding new ones by trial is slow. The pair trained a neural network to guess a eutectic's make-up and melting point from basic atomic traits alone.

Training data came from the ASM International phase diagram database: about 1,300 two-metal eutectics, cleaned for accuracy. Inputs ran from atomic number and weight to radius, electron traits and grip on electrons. The network beat random guessing and reached up to 11 percent accuracy under some settings, far short of the 80 percent target. Tests that dropped one input at a time fingered atomic radius and valence electron count as critical. Adding each metal's own melting point helped greatly, a clue for the next attempt.
doe-osti-3011884-securing-solar-for-the-:
Cybersecurity for solar and distributed energy resources is the subject of the Securing Solar for the Grid final project slides, DOE/GO-102025-6677. Danish Saleem led the National Renewable Energy Laboratory team from October 2021 to September 2024. The program aimed at high cybersecurity maturity across gear, supply chains, and grid work.

The team led work on the UL 2941 certification standard among manufacturers, utilities, installers, and aggregators. Firms and grid operators had a hand in that standards work, as did labs. The IEEE 1547.3 cybersecurity guide published in December 2023 and entered the IEEE 1547 revision timeline. Risk profiles for DERMS and supply chain guidance also came out of the work.
doe-osti-3015285-aligned-carbon-nanotube: Aligned carbon nanotubes for computing are the subject of a short CRADA final report, LBNL-2001736, dated December 30, 2025. Berkeley Lab contact Melanie Sonsteng ran the lab side, with Aligned Carbon Inc. under Cyclotron Road. Funding totaled 200,000 dollars. The firm grows aligned, uniform nanotubes on wafers. It purifies out metallic tubes, leaving semiconducting ones for transistor channels in computing and biosensing. Work centered on substrate preparation, synthesis, and post-processing toward foundry-ready production. The brief close-out form records no publications and no subject inventions.
doe-osti-3016977-s4pst-stewardship-and-a:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2026/4406, by Keita Teranishi, William Godoy, Pedro Valero Lara, and many colleagues, reports the S4PST project for 2024 and 2025. S4PST stewards programming systems and tools for high-performance computing. It is one of the software stewardship organizations funded under the federal Next Generation Scientific Software Technologies program.

The core portfolio under stewardship includes OpenMP, OpenACC, Kokkos, Fortran, LLVM, Legion, GASNet-EX, Open MPI, and MPICH. Incubation work covered Julia, Mojo for Python users, artificial intelligence in computing, and automatic differentiation. One highlight: the Enzyme compiler plugin makes adjoint calculations on graphics processors workable where standard methods run out of memory. The report also covers partnerships, workforce training, and software sustainability practice. Computing centers get a status record for tools their scientists depend on daily.
doe-osti-3021820-development-of-ionic-ba:
Oklahoma State University final technical report for DOE Geothermal Technologies award DE-EE0009788, led by Mohammed F. Al Dushaishi with Geir Hareland, Hunjoo P. Lee, and Prem Bikkina, covers May 2022 to July 2025 work on better fluids for enhanced geothermal systems. In these systems, water is pumped through hot fractured rock, and how the fluid spreads through fractures decides how much heat is harvested. The team synthesized ionic liquids and compared alternatives to steer that flow.

The synthesized ionic liquids began decomposing between 220 and 403 degrees Celsius, hot enough for geothermal service, and their non-volatility aids safety. Toxicity screening flagged one compound, HPyBr, as environmentally hazardous, prompting a prevention, containment, and treatment strategy and testing of oil-based and water-based alternatives. Under high-pressure, high-temperature tests, the fluids showed shear-thinning behavior; diluted ionic liquids flowed almost like water while staying stable to 470 degrees Fahrenheit.
doe-osti-3021836-computational-modeling-:
Texas Southern University final technical report for DOE award SC0023153, led by Bruce Prince with Daniel Vrinceanu and Mark Harvey. It closes a Research Development and Partnership Pilot project on atmospheric processes over Southeast Texas. Partners at Brookhaven National Laboratory and St. Edward's University joined TSU faculty and a large team of undergraduate and graduate student researchers. The science used data from DOE's ARM TRACER field campaign in the Houston area.

Students correlated fine particle pollution with the cloud condensation nuclei that seed convective clouds, using particle sizers and optical counters. A decade of air quality records, sorted by self-organizing maps of weather regimes, showed post-trough and anticyclonic patterns most tied to high ozone. Tethered balloon profiles linked atmospheric stability to pollutant trapping. The report is as much a training record as a science one, with student posters listed throughout.
doe-osti-3029249-release-of-evaluated-mi:
Denise Neudecker and twelve colleagues at Los Alamos National Laboratory document a nuclear data release in report LA-UR-26-22713, dated March 2026. Their subject is the average prompt fission neutron multiplicity for the minor plutonium isotopes 238, 240, 241, and 242. The values feed ENDF/B-IX.0, a standard library of evaluated nuclear data. For each isotope the team had four candidate evaluations and picked one.

Each pick rests on measured data plus model values from the CGMF code. The team chose the evaluations that matched measured data best and stayed smooth across energy. They then checked the chosen values against critical assembly results, from thermal to fast neutron energies above 5 MeV. Changes for plutonium-240 and 241 drove most of the shift seen in one benchmark case.
doe-osti-3377235-exploring-the-energy-fr:
Final technical report DOE-NEU-21174, dated June 2026, closes Louise Skinnari's Early Career award DE-SC0021174 at Northeastern University. The work ran from September 2020 to December 2025. It used the CMS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Two fronts shared the grant: hunts for new physics in top quarks and Higgs bosons, and faster tracking for the High-Luminosity LHC upgrade.

The flagship hunt sought charged lepton flavor violation in top decays. Using the full Run-2 data set, it set the world's strongest limits yet on the t to e-mu-q branching fraction. A second line built methods for a boosted top-pair-plus-Higgs measure of the top Yukawa coupling. On the hardware side, the team shaped the Level-1 track finder for the upgraded CMS. New trigger logic, among it a displaced vertex trigger, opens searches for long-lived particles that older triggers missed.
doe-osti-3382672-advanced-conductor-test:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-91884, dated April 2026, tests an advanced transmission conductor: a 1431 kcmil Prysmian ACSS conductor with E3X coating. Five authors are printed: Crash Bell, Steven K. Cook, Nikki Rasmussen, Abby M. Neumann, and Jake P. Gentle, of the laboratory's Advanced Grid Solutions group. An inner report dated January 2026 carries the fire testing processes and performance results.

Advanced conductors use composite cores, high-strength steel, and heat-dissipating coatings to carry more current with less sag at high temperature than the standard ACSR design. Utilities see them as a short to mid-term way to raise transmission capacity by reconductoring existing lines, before new lines can be built for growing loads such as data centers. Fire exposure is one of the hazards the test program puts the conductor through.
doe-osti-3409105-probabilistic-resource-:
Dated August 2026, report NLR/TP-6A40-100178 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies documents PRAS version 0.8, a tool for checking whether power systems have enough resources. Julian Florez, Srihari Sundar, Surya Chandan Dhulipala, and Gord Stephen wrote the guide. PRAS works with chance, not single fixed cases.

Worked examples show how to read loss of load chance by hour. One example checks unserved energy by region at a set hour in 2020. If only one region shows unserved energy, the fault is local, not system-wide. Grid planners can use such clues to target fixes where shortages truly sit.
doe-osti-3740376-justifi-the-project-val:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2026/4646 is the full user guide for JUSTIFI, a free project valuation tool. Seven authors from Oak Ridge and the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote it, led by Leslie Jones, Kristina Armstrong, and Mark Root. The tool serves the Department of Energy's Industrial Technologies Office software set. Plant teams often struggle to win approval for energy upgrades on energy savings alone. JUSTIFI counts the wider gains: safety, quality, less downtime, and higher output.

Users log a project's side benefits and tie each to measures their plant already tracks. The guide walks through setup, data entry, and the reports the tool produces. A worked example follows a cocoa company through a full assessment. Side material covers terms, links, and lean charts. The guide targets assessors, plant engineers, energy managers, and finance staff.
doe-osti-3818146-geologic-enhanced-mappi:
Official rules dated September 2026 set out the Geologic Enhanced Mapping System Prize, an American-Made contest. No author is named. The prize asks solvers to find hidden faults in geophysical survey data. Faults channel hot water underground, so mapping them points geothermal drillers toward strong sites. Entrants send fault maps for the GeoDAWN study area at one hundred metre grid size. Scoring uses a distance-weighted index.

The prize pool totals three hundred thousand dollars across two phases. Phase one pays fifty thousand, split among the top five entries on a hidden test set. Experts then fold the best entries into an updated fault label set. Phase two pays two hundred fifty thousand among the top five on that fuller set. The contest runs on the DrivenData platform. Training labels come from the INGENIOUS Great Basin data project.
doe-osti-3826913-nsuf-boiler-hfir-irradi:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2026/4858, dated September 2026, reports Fiscal Year 2026 progress on the BOILER irradiation study. Eight authors are printed, led by Kory Linton, Nick Russell, and Ethan Blount. The study tests two alumina-forming steels under neutron exposure plus liquid lead contact. Twenty-four small tensile samples and sixteen silicon carbide heat monitors rode in eight reactor capsules. Target heats were four hundred and six hundred fifty degrees Celsius.

All eight capsules were opened in a hot cell during the year, and every sample and monitor came out. Monitors went to a partner lab for sectioning and heat readout, still in progress. Samples were cleaned of clinging lead, weighed, and hardness-checked, all twenty-four of them. The report holds back the heat and hardness findings for later. Pull testing waits until the true irradiation heats are pinned down.
doe-osti-3827852-a-framework-for-validat:
Sandia report SAND2026-26269, printed September 2026, sets a validation frame for infrasound travel forecasts. Elizabeth Silber is the sole printed author. Infrasound, sound too low to hear, carries news of blasts and other events across whole regions. Treaty monitors lean on forecasts to link signals to sources and judge what stations should detect. Forecast tools differ, yet their inputs and settings are often logged loosely. Two honest models can then look in conflict when the records, not the physics, diverge.

The frame sorts checks into four stages: code verification, controlled model match-ups, replays of past events, and a semi-blind skill test. Air data enter as fixed, versioned benchmark packs, so every team plays the same sky. Source facts, station outcomes, and failure labels all get standard forms. Doubt ranges must be stated, not hidden. Tiered conformance lets weak and strong claims sit apart.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-fb:
On April 14, 2004, the Federal Bureau of Investigation sent the National Commission on Terrorist Attacks a report on its counterterrorism program since September 2001. The report tells the commission what the bureau changed after the attacks. It is a self-account, written for the body charged with judging the failure.

Joint Terrorism Task Forces stand near the center of the account. The report says their count rose from 34 to 84, with boards of local and federal chiefs in each field office. It also tells of a new Office of Law Enforcement Coordination, set up in the spring of 2002. The pages argue that these joint teams now sit at the heart of each terrorism case in the country.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in: One witness fills this short Federal Bureau of Investigation interview record from April 2002. Mr. McAlear flew for America West Airlines and taught part time at a flight school in Tempe, Arizona. Before that, he taught at Jet Tech International in Phoenix. There, in early 2001, he gave ground school training to Hani Hanjour, one of the men who later flew a hijacked plane. As freed, the file states who McAlear was and what he taught Hanjour. It gives little more of what he told the agents.

April 2004 dates this Federal Bureau of Investigation interview record in the set kept for the September 11 commission work. One name can be read in the garbled text layer: Bazarah, who was told who the agents were and why they had come, and then gave an account. Past that, the page is a wash of broken codes and split words. No place, subject, or claim in the talk can be recovered with trust. The file proves an interview was held that spring. Its substance is not legible here.

A short cable to all field offices, sent by the Usama Bin Laden unit of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in April 2001, fills this file. Its aim was to urge each office chief to keep up forward work against Bin Laden and Al Qaeda. The cable says the intelligence community judged that the threat of attacks on United States sites, staff, and interests would rise in the coming weeks, with Sunni extremists named as the source. The file as freed ends there, five months before the September attacks.

A lead to the bureau's Ottawa office opens this Federal Bureau of Investigation cable from San Diego, dated April 11, 2002. San Diego asked that Canadian service providers be pressed to name the user of a set of internet addresses. The lead rests on a car found the day after the attacks.

At 3:45 p.m. on September 12, 2001, airport police told the Washington office of a suspect car at Dulles airport. It sat in the hourly lot, row G: a 1988 Toyota Corolla with California plates. The cable then widens the point. The bureau held that the hijackers used email and the internet to plan and to talk. At least twelve of them, it says, bought tickets online, with email addresses left as contact points.

Los Angeles sent this Federal Bureau of Investigation cable on April 2, 2003, under the name Abdulaziz Al-Roomi. The case head ties him to Bin Laden and Al Qaeda work. The cable is classed secret in its whole. What survives in the text layer is the frame alone: routing lines, classification stamps, and page heads sent again and again. The body does not come through in readable form. It does not state what the bureau held against him.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-th:
A cable dated April 13, 2001, from the Usama Bin Laden unit opens this Federal Bureau of Investigation threat file. It went to every field office chief. Its point was sharp work against Bin Laden, and it pointed to fresh planning by his lieutenant Abu Zubaida as proof of the need.

The body reports a plot in the making. It says Al Qaeda men, Abu Zubaida among them, were at work on plans in more than one part of the world. Men and goods moved between Afghanistan, the Arabian peninsula, and Europe. Support tasks, it says, had to be done in the next few weeks. One report held that the group was far along in plans for an attack on United States interests in Saudi Arabia, with arms and explosives on the move.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pre-Assassinati: Rohm & Haas / US Navy Mixed Document Compilation (Part 2): the mixed compilation of company and Navy documents. A jumble, kept. A single compilation, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers. Readers will find it rewarding.
illustrated-history-of-furniture-from-th:
Frederick Litchfield traced furniture design from the earliest times to his own day in this illustrated history of 1893. The preface says most examples shown are of proven age and can be seen in museums. Room views show how pieces sat together in each period.

Litchfield links changes in furniture to social and historical change in each nation. Later pages turn to Japan and its art goods, little exported before the country opened. Alcock's work on Japanese craft is noted. Readers get both a picture survey and a plain account of why styles shifted.
nasa-tm-19660001399-nimbus-hrir-equipmen:
Howard R Stagner at Goddard wrote this August 1965 guide to a diagnostic test program for the Nimbus weather satellite. HRIR was its high resolution infrared radiometer, an instrument that maps heat from Earth. The program checks and maintains that equipment inside the Nimbus digitizing system, the catalog note says. Stagner sets out the program description first.

Operating steps, run modes, and input codes follow in order. A diagnostic program finds faults before flight data are lost. Ground crews needed clear steps they could run without the designer present. Manuals like this one kept complex ground systems usable, long after the people who built them moved on.
nasa-tm-19670024610-magnetic-computer-ta:
Virgil H. Byrd, of the Control Equipment Branch, wrote this report on saving worn magnetic computer tapes. Tapes lose signal in drop-outs, and new tapes cost money. Byrd reviews why tapes fail and how cleaning can bring used ones back.

The report sorts drop-outs into three types: contamination, oxide roughness, and backing damage. It then gives wet and dry cleaning methods and a testing routine. Suggested processes, Byrd reports, rehabilitate used tapes at about one-third the cost of new ones. Tables of pilot run results are included so other centers could judge the payoff.
nasa-tm-19710022937-a-comparison-of-vlf-:
R. A. Hoffman and Thomas Laaspere wrote this NASA preprint in August 1971, numbered X-646-71-319, on auroral hiss. The hiss is a very low frequency radio noise common over the polar regions. The authors wanted to pin down what generates it, using matched records from two experiments aboard the OGO-4 satellite.

One instrument listened for the hiss while another counted low-energy electrons falling into the atmosphere. On Earth's dayside, hiss occurrence matched events in the softest electron channel well, but matched higher-energy activity poorly. Exact matches between hiss intensity and electron flux were rare even in that channel. The authors conclude that dayside hiss is generated by soft cusp-region electrons. They add that the weak detailed match comes from the hiss spreading as it travels downward.
rinkitink-in-oz-wherein-is-recorded-the-:
L. Frank Baum, who signs himself Royal Historian of Oz, introduces this Oz tale in a letter from Ozcot, at Hollywood in California, in 1916. Its full title records the perilous quest of Prince Inga of Pingaree and King Rinkitink, in the magical isles beyond the Borderland of Oz. The boy hero is new, Baum warns his readers.

Dorothy is in the story too, and some of the company wander far from the Land of Oz. All assemble at last in the Emerald City for Ozma's banquet. Baum answers his readers' letters as fast as he can, he says, and asks them to write often. The chapter list begins with The Prince of Pingaree.
the-relations-between-religion-and-scien: Frederick, Lord Bishop of Exeter, preached eight Bampton Lectures before the University of Oxford in 1884, reprinted by Macmillan in a 1903 issue. An extract from John Bampton's will explains the trust that funds the lectures, directing rents from his estates to endow eight divinity lectures at Oxford forever. Here only the title pages and opening of that will extract are present, so the lectures themselves do not appear.
